Key Points
  • The passage describes Federico Ardila-Mantilla as a student who was not performing well in most subjects except for math.
  • The word "indifferent" accurately reflects his lack of engagement or interest in other subjects, which aligns with his overall poor school performance.
  • Other options such as "apprehensive", "apologetic", and "excellent" do not appropriately capture the context of his academic indifference in subjects other than math.
Therefore, the correct answer is 'Option 3'.
 
Complete Passage: The mathematician Federico Ardila-Mantilla grew up in Colombia, an indifferent student but gifted in math. He was failing most of his classes at his high school in Bogotá when someone encouraged him to apply to MIT. He had not heard of the school. To his surprise, he got in, and he went on scholarship. Mathematically, he did well. One of his professors, an acid-tongued theoretician known to liken his audience to a herd of cows, routinely tucked 'open' math problems into homework assignments, without telling the students. These had never been solved by anyone. Ardila solved one. He went on to receive his bachelor's and Ph.D. in math from MIT. But his academic experience was also one of isolation. Part of it had to do with his own shyness. Part of it was cultural. As a Latino, he was very much in the minority in the department, and he did not feel comfortable in American mathematical spaces. No one had tried to explicitly exclude him, yet he felt alone. In math, collaborating with others opens up new kinds of learning and thinking. But in his nine years at MIT, Ardila worked with others only twice.
 
Additional Information
  • Apprehensive (सशंकित): "Apprehensive" means anxious or fearful about something, which does not fit the context of discussing a lack of academic engagement.
  • Apologetic (क्षमाप्रार्थी): "Apologetic" means showing regret or remorse, which does not align with the context of the passage.
  • Excellent (उत्कृष्ट): "Excellent" means extremely good, which does not reflect the poor academic performance described.

He was failing most of his classes at his high school in Bogotá when someone suggested him to apply to MIT. He had not heard of the school. To his surprise, he got in, and he went on scholarship. Mathematically, he did well. One of his professors, an acid-tongued theoretician known to compare his audience to a herd of cows, routinely tucked 'open' math problems into homework assignments, without telling the students. These had never been solved by anyone. Ardila solved one. He went on to receive his bachelor's and Ph.D. in math from MIT. But his academic experience was also one of isolation. Part of it had to do with his own introversion. Part of it was cultural. As a Latino, he was very much in the minority in the department, and he did not feel comfortable in American mathematical spaces. No one had tried to explicitly exclude him, yet he felt alone. In math, collaborating with others opens up new kinds of learning and thinking. But in his nine years at MIT, Ardila worked with others only twice.
 
Additional Information

  • Incorporate (शामिल करना): 'Incorporate' means to include or integrate, which is the opposite of the idea of exclusion.
  • Stratify (विभाजित करना): 'Stratify' means to arrange or classify, which is unrelated to the context.

Therefore, the correct sentence is: "I am proud to belong to a religion which has taught the world both tolerance and universal acceptance," he declared on September 11, 1893. "We believe not only in universal toleration, but we accept all religions as true. I am proud to belong to a nation which has sheltered the persecuted and the (5) _________ of all religions and all nations of the earth."

Additional Information

  • Yet: This word often signals a contrast or an unexpected turn, but it doesn't pair naturally with "not only" in this context.
  • Though: Similar to "yet," "though" could signal a contrast, but it's not the standard word used to pair with "not only." It doesn't provide the same clear emphasis that "but" does.
  • And: This conjunction doesn't emphasize the surprising or unexpected nature of the second part of the statement in the way that "but" does. It simply links the two parts without adding any particular emphasis or contrast.
